title: The Effects of Outdoor Air Supply Rate in an Office on Perceived Air Quality, Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) Symptoms and Productivity

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: percentage of subjects dissatisfied with perceived air quality (upon entering initially, without bioeffluents)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality due to higher outdoor air supply.
findings.quote: an increased ventilation rate significantly improved the acceptability of the air quality (P<0.002)

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: perceived air freshness (upon entering initially, without bioeffluents)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality due to higher outdoor air supply.
findings.quote: and perceived air freshness (P<0.05)

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: odour intensity (upon entering initially, without bioeffluents)
findings.mechanism: Dilution of indoor pollutants by higher outdoor air supply.
findings.quote: reduced odour intensity (P<0.02)

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: nose irritation (upon entering initially, without bioeffluents)
findings.mechanism: Dilution of indoor pollutants by higher outdoor air supply.
findings.quote: and tended to reduce nose irritation (P<0.07)

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: percentage of subjects dissatisfied with perceived air quality (during exposure, with bioeffluents)
findings.mechanism: The presence of bioeffluents during exposure may have masked the effect.
findings.quote: during the exposure, the differences in perceived air quality between conditions did not reach statistical significance

findings.antecedent: lower ventilation rates (3 and 10 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: throat irritation (during exposure, with bioeffluents)
findings.mechanism: Higher concentrations of pollutants at lower ventilation rates likely cause irritation.
findings.quote: except for throat irritation which increased slightly during the exposure at 3 and 10 L/s per person (P<0.03)

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: percentage of subjects dissatisfied with perceived air quality (upon re-entering, with bioeffluents)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality due to higher outdoor air supply.
findings.quote: an increased ventilation rate significantly improved the acceptability of the air quality (P<0.01)

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: odour intensity (upon re-entering, with bioeffluents)
findings.mechanism: Dilution of indoor pollutants by higher outdoor air supply.
findings.quote: and tended to reduce odour intensity (P<0.10)

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: sensation of dry throat
findings.mechanism: Reduced concentrations of pollutants at higher ventilation rates.
findings.quote: The sensation of dry throat and mouth... were all significantly affected by changing the ventilation rate (P<0.001).

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: sensation of dry mouth
findings.mechanism: Reduced concentrations of pollutants at higher ventilation rates.
findings.quote: The sensation of dry throat and mouth... were all significantly affected by changing the ventilation rate (P<0.001).

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: difficulty in thinking clearly
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality reduces cognitive load and enhances mental clarity.
findings.quote: difficulty in thinking clearly... were all significantly affected by changing the ventilation rate (P<0.001).

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: general feeling of wellbeing (feeling bad/good)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality contributes to a better overall sense of well-being.
findings.quote: the general feeling of wellbeing (feeling good/bad) were all significantly affected by changing the ventilation rate (P<0.001).

findings.antecedent: lower ventilation rates (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: magnitude of fatigue
findings.mechanism: Worse air quality at lower ventilation rates contributes to increased fatigue.
findings.quote: The magnitude of fatigue and depression changed little with ventilation rate, although these symptoms were significantly worse when the ventilation rate was reduced (P<0.04).

findings.antecedent: lower ventilation rates (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: magnitude of depression
findings.mechanism: Worse air quality at lower ventilation rates contributes to increased depression.
findings.quote: The magnitude of fatigue and depression changed little with ventilation rate, although these symptoms were significantly worse when the ventilation rate was reduced (P<0.04).

findings.antecedent: changing the ventilation rate
findings.consequent: other SBS symptoms (not specified)
findings.mechanism: Only specific SBS symptoms were significantly affected.
findings.quote: Changing the ventilation rate did not significantly affect other SBS symptoms assessed during the exposure.

findings.antecedent: lower ventilation rates (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: effort required to complete performance tasks
findings.mechanism: Poorer air quality at lower ventilation rates increases perceived cognitive effort.
findings.quote: subjects tended to mark the scale closer to the “strong effort” end at lower ventilation rates (P<0.07).

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: overall performance in text typing task (integrating speed and accuracy)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality enhances cognitive function and reduces distractions, leading to better performance.
findings.quote: The results shown in Figure 6 confirm the results of the Page test and reach formal significance in the case of text typing (P<0.03).

findings.consequent: overall performance in text typing task
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality enhances cognitive function and reduces distractions, leading to better performance.
findings.quote: every two-fold increase in ventilation rate above 3 L/s per person would produce a 1.1% increase in overall performance in the text typing task

findings.consequent: overall performance in addition task (integrating speed and accuracy)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality enhances cognitive function and reduces distractions, leading to better performance.
findings.quote: A similar tendency was seen for the number of units completed per hour in the addition task (P<0.06)

findings.consequent: overall performance in addition task
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality enhances cognitive function and reduces distractions, leading to better performance.
findings.quote: and a 2.1% increase in overall performance in the addition and proof-reading tasks.

findings.consequent: overall performance in proof-reading task (integrating speed and accuracy)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality enhances cognitive function and reduces distractions, leading to better performance.
findings.quote: and the number of lines read per minute in the proof-reading task (P<0.07).

findings.consequent: overall performance in proof-reading task
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality enhances cognitive function and reduces distractions, leading to better performance.
findings.quote: and a 2.1% increase in overall performance in the addition and proof-reading tasks.

findings.antecedent: every two-fold increase of the ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: overall performance of subjects on all tasks (weighted by time spent)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality enhances cognitive function and reduces distractions, leading to better performance.
findings.quote: the overall performance of the subjects on all tasks by 1.4% if effects are weighted by the time spent on each performance task

findings.antecedent: every two-fold increase of the ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: overall performance of subjects on all tasks (unweighted mean workrate)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality enhances cognitive function and reduces distractions, leading to better performance.
findings.quote: or by 1.7% if an unweighted mean workrate is derived instead.

findings.antecedent: ventilation rate increased from 3 to 10 L/s per person
findings.consequent: number of alternative uses for specified objects (creative thinking task)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality may facilitate divergent thinking and creative output.
findings.quote: subjects wrote down more alternative uses of specified objects (P<0.025)

findings.antecedent: higher ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: originality score of alternative uses (creative thinking task)
findings.mechanism: Improved air quality may facilitate divergent thinking and creative output.
findings.quote: a significantly higher score was obtained at the higher ventilation rate (P<0.046)

findings.antecedent: ventilation rate further, from 10 to 30 L/s per person
findings.consequent: number of alternative uses or originality score (creative thinking task)
findings.mechanism: The benefits for creative thinking may plateau at certain ventilation rates.
findings.quote: Increasing ventilation rate further, from 10 to 30 L/s per person, had no significant effect on either of these measures.

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate (3 to 30 L/s per person)
findings.consequent: average metabolic rate of the subjects
findings.mechanism: Increased muscle tonus at higher work rates or unconscious reduction of breathing rate at low ventilation rates.
findings.quote: These values increase systematically with ventilation rate (Page test, P<0.05).

findings.antecedent: increased ventilation rate
findings.consequent: sensory pollution loads from materials
findings.mechanism: Materials may emit more pollutants at higher ventilation rates due to increased air movement or other factors.
findings.quote: The present results show that the sensory pollution loads from materials may not always be constant... but can increase with increasing ventilation rate

stimuli.description: A normally furnished office space (108 m³) with a carpet as an extra pollution source, ventilated with outdoor airflow of 3, 10 or 30 L/s per person. Temperature 22°C, RH 40%, air velocity <0.2 m/s, noise 42 dB(A) were kept constant.

limitations: Generalizability to other populations (males, older, different occupations) due to use of young female students.
The experimental office space may have been perceived as different from a normal workplace.
Subjects were exposed only once to each condition for a short period (ca. 4.6 h), unlike real-world repeated, longer exposures.
The 'task difficulty or necessary effort' scale was found to be difficult for subjects to use and its interpretation ambiguous, suggesting it should not be used in its present form.
